historical_timeline.summary: Adopted into the Shiobara family; returned to his birth family at nine.
Graduates from the Imperial University; later teaches in Matsuyama and Kumamoto and marries.
Sent to Britain to study English; severe nervous distress there; returns in 1903.
Joins the Asahi Shimbun as a staff writer; moves to Waseda-Minami-chō.
Admitted to the Nagayo Gastrointestinal Hospital; discharged July 31.
Massive hemorrhage and critical illness at Shuzenji (the Shuzenji crisis).
Hemorrhoids, nervous distress and diabetes in his later years (dates not given).
Dies at home in Waseda after a recurrence of the ulcer with internal bleeding.

claims.statement: Natsume Sōseki, whose name was Natsume Kinnosuke, was born on the 5th day of the 1st month of Keiō 3 in the Japanese calendar (9 February 1867) in Ushigome Babashita-Yokomachi in Edo, now Kikui-chō in Shinjuku, Tokyo, the son of a town headman.
At the age of one he was adopted into the Shiobara family; his adoptive parents divorced when he was nine, and he was returned to his birth family.

After graduating from the English department of the Imperial University in 1893 he taught at Matsuyama Middle School and at the Fifth Higher School in Kumamoto, and married Nakane Kyōko, eldest daughter of Nakane Shigeichi, chief secretary of the House of Peers, after taking up the Kumamoto post.
claims.clinical_interpretation: History only; his wife is not given any role in the modern episode.

claims.statement: In 1900, at 33, he was sent by the Ministry of Education to Britain to study English for two years, and he returned to Japan in 1903.
During his stay in Britain he soon felt at odds with the study of English literature and fell into a state of severe nervous distress, which continued after his return.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Past history of documented distress; no modern psychiatric diagnosis is asserted.

claims.statement: The city of Shinjuku calls the London illness shinkei suijaku (nervous breakdown, neurasthenia), and the Sōseki museum calls it nervous depression; both are labels of the period or translations of it, not modern diagnoses.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective labels; the modern episode records only distress, not a diagnosis.

claims.statement: In 1907, at 40, he gave up all his teaching posts and joined the Asahi Shimbun as a staff writer, and about then moved to Waseda-Minami-chō; Sanshirō, Sorekara and Mon were serialized in the newspaper. He had made his name with I Am a Cat (1905 to 1906) and later wrote Kokoro (1914).
From about May 1910, while writing Mon, he suffered from stomach illness, a gastric ulcer.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The anchor for the index visit and the synthetic presenting illness.

claims.statement: On 18 June 1910 he entered the Nagayo Gastrointestinal Hospital in Tokyo, and he was discharged on 31 July.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the index date; no modern visit is placed during the stay.

claims.statement: On 6 August 1910 he went to Shuzenji in Izu for a change of air; there he vomited a large amount of blood and fell into a critical condition but survived. His diary record marks 24 August 1910 as the day he was critically ill, the entry written for him by his wife.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the index date; the Shuzenji crisis. No modern visit is placed after August 5.

claims.statement: In his later years he suffered, besides the gastric ulcer, from hemorrhoids and nervous distress, and developed diabetes.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the index date; the dates are not given in the cited source.

claims.statement: In 1916, while he was writing Meian (Light and Dark), the gastric ulcer recurred with internal bleeding, and he died at his home in Waseda-Minami-chō on 9 December 1916, at 49, leaving the novel unfinished.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Recognize a bleeding peptic ulcer in a 43-year-old novelist in Tokyo with epigastric pain, black stools and iron-deficiency anemia, and care for it as Japanese and international guidance advise: a Glasgow-Blatchford score and clear instructions on when to call 119; stopping NSAIDs; urgent upper endoscopy with biopsy of the ulcer margin to exclude gastric cancer, which is common in Japan, and mapping biopsies for Helicobacter pylori and atrophy; acid suppression with vonoprazan; H. pylori eradication chosen by local resistance and the patient's own susceptibility result (vonoprazan-amoxicillin dual therapy for a clarithromycin-resistant strain, because bismuth quadruple therapy is not available for this use in Japan); confirmation of eradication by urea breath test off acid suppression; repeat endoscopy to confirm healing of a gastric ulcer; oral iron with monitoring of the blood count (CMID anemia monograph); advice on alcohol and smoking; stress and depression screening; and endoscopic surveillance for gastric cancer after eradication because of atrophy and intestinal metaplasia. The modern episode is a teaching case, not a claim about the cause of his real illness.

documentation.chief_complaint: Three-day review, with upper endoscopy by gastroenterology this morning

hpi.narrative: Mr. Natsume returns three days after his first visit and had an upper endoscopy this morning with Dr. Abrahamsen-Ito of gastroenterology. Since his first visit he has stopped ibuprofen and taken acetaminophen twice for headache. The epigastric pain continues, gnawing before meals and waking him at night, and is eased by food. His stools have been brown, with no further black stools since ten days before his first visit, and he has not vomited blood or felt faint. He fasted for the endoscopy and has recovered from the sedation.

assessment_plan.assessment: Endoscopy shows a 15 mm ulcer on the lesser curvature at the angulus with a clean white base (Forrest III), regular margins and smooth converging folds, which look benign; there is no blood in the stomach and the duodenum is normal. A clean base carries a low risk of rebleeding, and with a stable hemoglobin of 11.0 g/dL and normal pulse and blood pressure he can be treated at home. Six biopsies of the ulcer margin were taken because a gastric ulcer can hide a cancer, which is common in Japan. Dr. Abrahamsen-Ito and I agree the plan
plan: Vonoprazan 20 mg each morning for eight weeks, started after the biopsies
No NSAIDs; acetaminophen for pain
Call 119 for black, tarry stools, vomiting blood or coffee-ground material, or fainting
Biopsy results and the eradication plan at two weeks

Mapping biopsies for histology and a PCR test for clarithromycin resistance were sent; in Japan clarithromycin resistance is common, so treatment will be chosen when the result is back
plan: Eradication therapy at the two-week visit, chosen by the resistance result

hpi.narrative: Mr. Natsume returns two weeks after his endoscopy. The epigastric pain stopped within four days of starting vonoprazan, and he now sleeps through the night. His stools are dark and formed on iron, with no sticky, tarry stools; he has not vomited or felt faint. He takes the iron every other morning without stomach upset. He has taken no NSAIDs. He is writing his serial again each morning and eats at more regular hours.

documentation.chief_complaint: Low back pain for two days after lifting a box of books

hpi.narrative: Mr. Natsume called this morning and was seen the same day. Two days ago he lifted a heavy box of books from the floor of his study and felt a pull across his lower back. The pain is a dull ache across both sides of the low back, worse when he bends or gets up from the floor, and eased by lying on his side. It does not spread down his legs. He has no numbness, weakness, or trouble passing urine or stool, no fever, and no history of cancer. He wanted to take the ibuprofen he used to keep for headaches but remembered that he must not, and asks what he may take instead. He is on day eight of fourteen of his eradication therapy, taking every dose; he has slightly loose stools once a day and a metallic taste but no diarrhea, rash or abdominal pain. His stomach pain has gone, and his stools are dark from the iron but formed.

referral.question: Suspected bleeding peptic ulcer in a 43-year-old novelist with three weeks of epigastric pain, two black, tarry stools ten days ago, and iron-deficiency anemia, after occasional ibuprofen. Please perform upper endoscopy with biopsy, exclude gastric cancer, test for Helicobacter pylori, and advise on treatment and follow-up
referral.urgency: Urgent, within three days. He is stable today with no further black stools; Glasgow-Blatchford score 4 (hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL and the history of melena). He has been told to call 119 or go to the emergency department at once for black or bloody stools, vomiting blood or coffee-ground material, fainting, or severe pain. No acid suppression has been started, so that the biopsies are not affected, unless bleeding recurs
referral.pertinent_history: Gnawing epigastric pain for about three weeks, worse before meals and at night and eased by food, with two black, tarry stools ten days ago; none since. No vomiting, weight loss, difficulty swallowing or fainting. Ibuprofen 200 to 400 mg a few times a month for headaches, stopped today; acetaminophen instead. No tobacco; alcohol rarely. No known allergy. No earlier endoscopy or H. pylori testing. A period of severe nervous distress years ago during study abroad, now past; PHQ-9 7 and GAD-7 8 today, around work deadlines. Today: weight 52.0 kg (BMI 20.6), blood pressure 124/78, pulse 84, no postural symptoms; mild epigastric tenderness, no mass or lymph nodes. Hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL, MCV 76 fL, RDW 16.9%, platelets 418 x10^3/uL; ferritin 8 ng/mL, iron 38 ug/dL, transferrin saturation 8%; urea nitrogen 15 mg/dL, creatinine 0.92 mg/dL
questions: What is the source of the bleeding, and is this a peptic ulcer?
Can gastric cancer be excluded, and what biopsies are needed?
Does he have Helicobacter pylori, and which eradication regimen do you advise given clarithromycin resistance in Japan?
Can he be treated at home, and what acid suppression and follow-up endoscopy do you advise?
Does the iron-deficiency anemia need colonoscopy as well?
Does he need surveillance for gastric cancer after treatment?

consultant_note.history: Mr. Natsume, a 43-year-old novelist, is seen at the request of Dr. Lindqvist-Mori three days after his first visit. He describes three weeks of gnawing upper abdominal pain before meals and at night, relieved by food, and two black, tarry stools about two weeks ago, with none since. He had taken ibuprofen for headaches a few times a month and stopped it at his first visit. He has not vomited blood, lost weight, or had trouble swallowing. He does not smoke and rarely drinks. He has never had an endoscopy. He is worried about stomach cancer and wants to keep writing his newspaper serial
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Dr. Lindqvist-Mori's intake note and results: hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL with MCV 76 fL and ferritin 8 ng/mL; urea nitrogen 15 mg/dL; Glasgow-Blatchford score 4. Hemoglobin this morning 11.0 g/dL. Upper endoscopy this morning under light sedation: normal esophagus; a 15 mm ulcer on the lesser curvature at the angulus with a clean white base and no visible vessel or adherent clot (Forrest III), regular margins and smooth converging folds; open-type atrophy (Kimura-Takemoto O-1) with antral nodularity; no blood in the stomach; normal duodenum. Six biopsies were taken from the ulcer margin, five mapping biopsies (updated Sydney protocol) for histology, and a biopsy for clarithromycin-resistance PCR. Rapid urease test positive

exam.finding: Alert after light sedation; pale; pulse 82, blood pressure 122/76
Mild epigastric tenderness; no guarding, mass or enlarged liver
No supraclavicular node

assessment.assessment: The source is a 15 mm gastric ulcer at the angulus with a clean base, which carries a low risk of rebleeding and needs no endoscopic treatment. The likely causes are Helicobacter pylori and the ibuprofen. With a stable hemoglobin and normal pulse and blood pressure, he can be treated at home. The ulcer looks benign, but a gastric ulcer must be biopsied and followed to healing because an early gastric cancer can look like one

The rapid urease test is positive. Clarithromycin resistance is common in Japan, so the regimen should follow the PCR result: vonoprazan, amoxicillin and clarithromycin for 7 days if the strain is susceptible, or vonoprazan 20 mg twice daily with amoxicillin 1 g three times daily for 14 days if it is resistant. Bismuth quadruple therapy, preferred elsewhere when susceptibility is unknown, is not available for this use in Japan

Explained by the bleeding ulcer. In an adult man with iron-deficiency anemia a colonoscopy is usually advised too, but with an upper source found and no bowel symptoms it can wait to see whether the anemia corrects once the ulcer heals; if it does not, colonoscopy is needed

The open-type atrophy at endoscopy suggests long-standing infection; the mapping biopsies will stage atrophy and intestinal metaplasia. Eradication lowers the risk of gastric cancer but does not remove it when atrophy is extensive, so surveillance endoscopy is likely to be needed

recommendations: Start vonoprazan 20 mg each morning now, after the biopsies, and continue for eight weeks for a gastric ulcer
No NSAIDs, including aspirin and combination cold remedies; acetaminophen for pain; no smoking and little alcohol

Eradication at the two-week visit, chosen by the clarithromycin-resistance PCR: vonoprazan-amoxicillin dual therapy for 14 days if resistant, or vonoprazan triple therapy with clarithromycin for 7 days if susceptible
Confirm eradication with a 13C urea breath test at least four weeks after the antibiotics and at least two weeks after stopping vonoprazan
Repeat endoscopy at about ten weeks to confirm healing and to biopsy the scar
Oral iron from today; colonoscopy only if the anemia does not correct after the ulcer has healed
Endoscopic surveillance after eradication if the biopsies confirm atrophy or intestinal metaplasia: yearly is usual practice in Japan for moderate or extensive atrophy
Call 119 or go to the emergency department for black, tarry stools, vomiting blood or coffee-ground material, fainting, or sudden severe pain

The endoscopy pictures were shown to Mr. Natsume, who asked whether it was cancer; he was told that the ulcer looks benign and that the biopsies would answer the question in about two weeks
consultant_note.follow_up: Repeat endoscopy with Dr. Abrahamsen-Ito at about ten weeks, combined with the urea breath test; then yearly surveillance endoscopy if the histology confirms atrophy
